name: Fall Weiss: the invasion of Poland
intro: Germany attacked Poland from three sides at dawn on 1 September 1939, and the Soviet Union invaded from the east on 17 September. Poland's armies, spread out to cover the whole frontier, were outflanked and broken up in five weeks, though not without hard fighting.

phases.p: At 04:45 the battleship Schleswig-Holstein opens fire on Westerplatte and German armies cross the frontier. Army Group North cuts the Polish Corridor by 3 September and pushes south from East Prussia towards the Narew. Army Group South drives from Silesia and Slovakia: Polish cavalry and infantry fight hard at Mokra and in the Tuchola forest, but Kraków falls on 6 September and panzers race for Warsaw. Britain and France declare war on 3 September but do not attack in the west. Westerplatte surrenders on 7 September.

On 8 September the 4th Panzer Division reaches the south-western edge of Warsaw and is thrown back. Next day Kutrzeba's Army Poznań, bypassed in the west, strikes south across the Bzura into the flank of the German 8th Army. It becomes the largest battle of the campaign: German reinforcements and the Luftwaffe turn it into an encirclement, and by 19 September some 120,000 Poles have surrendered. In the east Guderian's corps drives behind the Bug to Brest, while Lwów is besieged.

At dawn on 17 September, under the secret protocol of the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, the Red Army's Belorussian and Ukrainian Fronts cross the eastern border, held only by thin Border Protection Corps units. Rydz-Śmigły orders his troops not to fight the Soviets except in self-defence, and that night the government crosses into Romania. Wilno falls on 19 September and Grodno, after a stubborn defence, on 22 September; Lwów surrenders to the Red Army the same day. At Brest German and Soviet troops hold a joint parade.

Warsaw, shelled and bombed for days and without water or power, capitulates on 28 September. The same day Germany and the Soviet Union sign the Boundary and Friendship Treaty, moving the dividing line east to the Bug and San in exchange for Lithuania. Modlin falls on 29 September and the Hel peninsula on 2 October. The last field force, Kleeberg's Independent Operational Group Polesie, fights at Kock from 2 to 5 October and surrenders on 6 October. Tens of thousands of Poles escape through Romania and Hungary to fight on.

name: Fall Gelb: Sedan and the race to the Channel
intro: The Allies expected the main German blow through central Belgium and rushed their best armies forward to meet it. Instead seven panzer divisions crossed the Ardennes, broke the French line on the Meuse and drove to the Channel, cutting the Allied armies in two.

phases.t: 10–12 May · into Belgium and the Ardennes
phases.p: Army Group B invades the Netherlands and Belgium; gliders land on Fort Eben-Emael and the Albert Canal bridges, and the fort surrenders on 11 May. As planned, the BEF and the French First Army advance to the Dyle line between Antwerp and Namur, and the French Seventh Army dashes towards Breda. Meanwhile Army Group A's Panzer Group Kleist threads the Ardennes forest roads in enormous columns. French light cavalry is pushed back, and by the evening of 12 May the panzers stand on the Meuse.

On 13 May hundreds of bombers and Stukas pound the French 55th Division at Sedan. That afternoon Guderian's infantry cross the Meuse in rubber boats near Glaire and Donchery and climb to the heights of La Marfée; in the evening panic spreads through the French artillery at Bulson. Rommel's 7th Panzer has already crossed at Houx near Dinant, and Reinhardt's corps fights over the river at Monthermé. At Gembloux the French First Army holds, but counter-attacks at Stonne fail and on 15 May the French 9th Army collapses.

phases.t: 16–21 May · the race to the sea
phases.p: The panzers turn west through open country with little in front of them. De Gaulle's 4th Armoured Division strikes the flank at Montcornet on 17 May without lasting effect. On 20 May the 2nd Panzer Division reaches Abbeville and its patrols reach the coast at Noyelles: the Allied northern armies are cut off. Next day British tanks and infantry counter-attack south of Arras against Rommel's 7th Panzer and the SS Totenkopf Division, causing alarm but no breakthrough. Weygand has replaced Gamelin on 19 May.

phases.t: 22–28 May · the Channel ports and the halt order
phases.p: Guderian swings north: the 2nd Panzer Division takes Boulogne by 25 May and the 10th Panzer Division takes Calais on 26 May after a stubborn British defence. On 24 May Hitler confirms Rundstedt's order halting the panzers on the Aa canal line, about 20 km from Dunkirk, for nearly three days. The BEF and French fall back into a corridor to the sea. Belgium capitulates on 28 May. At Le Paradis and Wormhoudt on 27–28 May British prisoners of the Royal Norfolks and Royal Warwicks are murdered after surrender.

Operation Dynamo begins on the evening of 26 May. Ships load from the beaches at Bray-Dunes, De Panne and Malo, and above all from Dunkirk's East Mole, while French and British rearguards hold the perimeter along the canals. The French First Army, trapped around Lille, fights on until 31 May and holds back several German divisions. By 4 June 338,226 men have been carried to England, about a third of them French. The last French defenders, some 35,000 men, are captured when Dunkirk falls that morning.

name: The Battle of Britain
intro: Before any invasion Germany had to beat the Royal Air Force. Fighter Command's radar-fed control system let Dowding fight a defensive battle over south-east England, with each group guarding its own part of the country and 11 Group in the front line.

phases.p: The Luftwaffe attacks convoys in the Channel and the port of Dover to draw the RAF into combat. Over 'Hellfire Corner' Luftflotte 2 flies from airfields in the Pas-de-Calais, while Luftflotte 3 operates from Normandy and Brittany. Dowding, at Fighter Command headquarters in Bentley Priory, refuses to commit large forces over the sea. Park's 11 Group, controlled from Uxbridge, bears the brunt, with 10 Group to the west and 12 Group north of the Thames. On 16 July Hitler orders preparations for Operation Sea Lion.

On 12 August raiders hit the radar stations at Dover, Rye, Pevensey and Dunkirk in Kent, knocking out Ventnor on the Isle of Wight, and bomb the forward airfields at Manston, Lympne and Hawkinge. Adlertag, the main assault, opens on 13 August. On 15 August the Luftwaffe flies more than 1,700 sorties, including raids from Norway on the north-east. On 18 August, 'the Hardest Day', Dorniers attack Kenley at low level and Stukas hit the Sussex and Hampshire airfields; their losses are so heavy that the Ju 87 is soon withdrawn.

Kesselring now sends bombers with heavy fighter escort against 11 Group's sector airfields. Biggin Hill is hit repeatedly between 30 August and 1 September and its operations room is wrecked; Hornchurch, North Weald, Debden and Kenley are also damaged, and Manston is all but abandoned. Fighter Command loses pilots faster than they can be replaced. On the night of 24–25 August stray bombs fall on central London; Bomber Command raids Berlin the following night, and on 4 September Hitler promises revenge.

On the afternoon of 7 September Göring switches the attack to London: some 350 bombers with over 600 fighters set the docks and East End ablaze, and the Blitz begins. The battered airfields recover. On Sunday 15 September two heavy raids are met by 11 Group squadrons along their whole route and by 12 Group's 'Big Wing' from Duxford. The Luftwaffe loses around 60 aircraft and its claim that the RAF is finished is exposed. On 17 September Hitler postpones Sea Lion indefinitely.

phases.t: 16 September – 31 October · fighter-bombers and the night
phases.p: Large daylight bomber raids become rarer after a costly defeat on 30 September. In October the Luftwaffe sends high-flying Bf 109 fighter-bombers, hard to intercept but carrying too little to do much damage, while its bombers turn to night attacks on London and other cities, against which the RAF as yet has little defence. The British date the end of the battle to 31 October. Some 2,900 Fighter Command aircrew, Churchill's 'Few', had flown in it, and Sea Lion was never launched.

name: Operation Barbarossa: from the border to Moscow
intro: More than three million German and allied troops invaded the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941. The Wehrmacht won the largest encirclement battles in history, but each one cost time, and the drive on Moscow ended in snow at the gates of the capital.

phases.t: 22 June – 9 July · the frontier and Minsk
phases.p: Before dawn on 22 June three army groups attack along the whole frontier. About 1,200 Soviet aircraft are lost on the first day, most of them on the ground, and the Brest fortress garrison fights on for weeks behind the front. Army Group Centre's two panzer groups, Hoth from the north and Guderian from the south, meet at Minsk on 28 June, trapping much of the Western Front in the Białystok and Minsk pockets; Germany claims some 320,000 prisoners. Pavlov, the front commander, is later shot.

The panzers cross the Dnieper and the Dvina and close a new pocket around Smolensk, which falls on 16 July. The Soviet armies inside fight on and part of them break out, while repeated counter-attacks around Yartsevo and Yelnya wear down Army Group Centre. In late August Hitler, against his generals' advice, turns Guderian south towards Ukraine and Hoth's tanks north. On 6 September Zhukov's Reserve Front retakes the Yelnya salient, the first time the Germans have been forced to give up ground.

Guderian's 2nd Panzer Group drives south from the Desna while Kleist's 1st Panzer Group strikes north from its Dnieper bridgehead at Kremenchug on 12 September. Stalin forbids Kirponos's Southwestern Front to withdraw. On 15 September the two pincers meet at Lokhvitsa, some 200 km east of Kiev. Kiev falls on 19 September and Kirponos is killed trying to break out. The Germans claim 665,000 prisoners, but the drive on Moscow has been delayed by about a month.

Typhoon opens on 30 September in the south and 2 October in the centre. Within a week double encirclements at Vyazma and Bryansk trap much of three Soviet fronts. Then the autumn rains turn the roads to mud. Zhukov takes over the defence of Moscow, and fresh divisions arrive from Siberia and the Far East. When frost hardens the ground the second assault in mid-November gets within about 30 km of the Kremlin and across the Moscow–Volga canal at Yakhroma, but Tula holds out.

In bitter cold the Kalinin Front attacks on 5 December and the Western Front the next day. German units without winter clothing, their weapons and engines freezing, fall back. Klin and Kalinin are retaken in mid-December and Kaluga on 30 December. Hitler issues a stand-fast order on 16 December, accepts Brauchitsch's resignation and takes personal command of the army; Guderian is dismissed on 25 December. By early January the Germans have been driven back 100 to 250 km from Moscow.

name: Stalingrad: the battle for the city
intro: Stalingrad stretched for some 40 km along the high west bank of the Volga. The German 6th Army fought for it street by street and factory by factory, while Chuikov's 62nd Army clung to a strip of ruins along the river, supplied across it at night.

phases.p: On 23 August the 16th Panzer Division drives some 60 km from its Don bridgehead and reaches the Volga just north of the city near Rynok, while Luftflotte 4 sets Stalingrad ablaze in a day of mass raids that kills thousands of civilians. Workers' militia and tanks straight from the tractor factory fight on the northern edge. In early September the 6th Army closes in from the west and the 4th Panzer Army from the south-west, reaching the Volga at Kuporosnoye on 10 September. Chuikov takes command of the 62nd Army on 12 September.

On 13 September the 6th Army storms the city centre. The 71st and 295th Infantry Divisions push for the central landing stage and Mamayev Kurgan, and the central station changes hands repeatedly. On the night of 14–15 September Rodimtsev's 13th Guards Rifle Division crosses the Volga under fire and is thrown straight into the fight. South of the Tsaritsa the grain elevator holds out for days against repeated assaults. By 26 September the Germans hold most of the centre, but not the riverbank.

Paulus shifts his weight north. From 27 September the Germans fight into the workers' settlements below the Red October, Barrikady and tractor factories and take the Orlovka salient. On 14 October, after an intense air and artillery bombardment, the 14th Panzer and 305th Infantry Divisions break through to the Volga at the tractor factory, cutting off the northern Soviet group at Spartanovka and Rynok. In the centre Sergeant Pavlov's platoon holds a block of flats on 9 January Square for about two months.

On 11 November Paulus launches his last assault, spearheaded by pioneer battalions flown in for street fighting, against the Barrikady and Red October factories. The Germans reach the Volga on a narrow front south of the Barrikady, isolating Colonel Lyudnikov's 138th Rifle Division on a strip of bank some 700 m long, 'Lyudnikov's Island', supplied across the ice-choked river. The attack bleeds out within days. On 19 November the Red Army launches Operation Uranus against the Romanian armies on the flanks.

phases.t: 10 January – 2 February 1943 · the end of the 6th Army
phases.p: Encircled since 23 November and starving, the 6th Army rejects surrender terms. Operation Koltso opens on 10 January from the west; the airfields at Pitomnik and Gumrak fall, and on 26 January the 21st Army meets Chuikov's men near Mamayev Kurgan and the Red October settlement, splitting the pocket in two. Paulus, promoted field marshal the day before, is taken in the basement of the Univermag department store on 31 January. Strecker's northern group in the tractor factory gives up on 2 February. About 91,000 prisoners go into captivity.

name: Operation Uranus: the encirclement at Stalingrad
intro: While the 6th Army was absorbed in the ruins of Stalingrad, the Red Army massed over a million men against its long flanks, held by poorly equipped Romanian armies. Operation Uranus encircled roughly 300,000 German and allied troops in four days.

phases.p: Army Group B's drive to the Volga has left a front of hundreds of kilometres along the Don and across the Kalmyk steppe. The 6th Army and part of the 4th Panzer Army are concentrated in and around Stalingrad, while the flanks are held by the Romanian 3rd Army on the Don and the Romanian 4th Army south of the city, short of anti-tank guns. The Soviets keep bridgeheads across the Don at Serafimovich and Kletskaya and from late October secretly mass tank and cavalry corps in them.

At 07:30 on 19 November an 80-minute bombardment opens in thick fog, and the 5th Tank and 21st Armies break out of the Don bridgeheads, shattering the Romanian 3rd Army. The weak German XLVIII Panzer Corps fails to stop them. Next day the Stalingrad Front attacks south of the city through the Romanian 4th Army. On 22 November the 26th Tank Corps seizes the Don bridge at Kalach intact, and on the afternoon of 23 November the 4th Tank and 4th Mechanised Corps meet at Sovetsky. The 6th Army is trapped.

phases.t: 12–24 December · Winter Storm and Little Saturn
phases.p: Hitler forbids a breakout, relying on Göring's promise of an airlift that delivers far less than the army needs. On 12 December Manstein's relief attack, Winter Storm, sets out from Kotelnikovo with the LVII Panzer Corps. After fierce tank battles on the Aksay it reaches the Myshkova river on 19 December, some 48 km from the pocket, but Paulus does not break out. Little Saturn, launched on 16 December, shatters the Italian 8th Army; on 24 December Soviet tanks overrun Tatsinskaya airfield, and the relief force must fall back.

With relief gone, the Don Front opens Operation Koltso on 10 January after Paulus rejects surrender terms. Attacking from the west, the 65th and 21st Armies take the Marinovka salient and on 16 January Pitomnik, the main airfield; Gumrak falls on 22 January. The shrinking pocket is split on 26 January. Paulus surrenders in the city centre on 31 January and the northern group on 2 February. By then the Soviet winter offensive has pushed the front far to the west, beyond the Donets.

name: Kursk and Prokhorovka
intro: The Kursk salient bulged some 150 km into the German line. Hitler's Operation Citadel aimed to pinch it off from north and south, but the Soviets, forewarned, waited behind the deepest field defences of the war with strong reserves ready for a counter-offensive.

phases.p: After the spring thaw both sides build up around the salient left by the winter fighting. Hitler postpones Citadel several times to wait for new Panther and Tiger tanks and Ferdinand tank destroyers. Rokossovsky's Central Front and Vatutin's Voronezh Front dig belt after belt of trenches, minefields and anti-tank strongpoints, with Konev's Steppe Front in reserve behind them. Model's 9th Army stands ready to attack from the north, and Hoth's 4th Panzer Army and Army Detachment Kempf from the south.

The attack opens on 5 July. In the north Model's infantry and tanks gain barely 12 km, stalling at Ponyri and the Olkhovatka heights. In the south the II SS Panzer Corps and XLVIII Panzer Corps grind through the first defence belts and push some 35 km towards Oboyan and Prokhorovka, while Kempf's III Panzer Corps, held up east of the Donets, struggles to cover their right flank. Losses mount on both sides; Vatutin commits his reserves and Steppe Front armies move up.

On 12 July Rotmistrov's 5th Guards Tank Army counter-attacks the II SS Panzer Corps on the fields south-west of Prokhorovka station. Charging into prepared positions near the Oktyabrsky state farm, the Soviet tank brigades lose several hundred tanks destroyed or damaged, against German losses of a few dozen, but the SS advance is halted. The same day the Western and Bryansk Fronts launch Operation Kutuzov against the Orel salient behind Model's 9th Army, forcing him onto the defensive.

On 13 July Hitler calls off Citadel, citing the Allied landings in Sicily, and Manstein's divisions fall back to their start lines. Orel and Belgorod are liberated on 5 August, celebrated in Moscow with the first artillery salute of the war. Operation Rumyantsev then drives on Kharkov; German counter-attacks around Bogodukhov and Akhtyrka slow it, but Kharkov changes hands for the last time on 23 August. From now on the strategic initiative in the east lies with the Red Army.

name: Monte Cassino and Anzio: the road to Rome
intro: Two fronts some 100 km apart fought as one battle. The Allies landed at Anzio to unhinge the Gustav Line; instead the beachhead was besieged, and the line at Cassino was broken only in May by a massive offensive that finally opened the road to Rome.

phases.t: 17–24 January · the Gustav Line and the Anzio landing
phases.p: British X Corps crosses the lower Garigliano on 17 January; on 20–22 January the US 36th Division is shattered trying to cross the Rapido near Sant'Angelo. These attacks are meant to draw German reserves south while VI Corps lands at Anzio and Nettuno at 02:00 on 22 January. The landing is almost unopposed, but Lucas consolidates his beachhead instead of striking for the Alban Hills, and Kesselring rushes in troops from all over Italy and beyond.

phases.t: 25 January – 20 February · deadlock on both fronts
phases.p: At Cassino the US 34th Division fights into the mountains north of the town and the French reach the Belvedere, but the abbey heights hold. On 15 February bombers destroy the abbey, and the 4th Indian Division then fails to take it. At Anzio the British push to Campoleone and the Rangers are destroyed near Cisterna on 30 January. On 16 February Mackensen's Fourteenth Army counter-attacks down the Via Anziate in Operation Fischfang and is stopped only at the Flyover on 19–20 February.

After heavy bombers flatten Cassino town on 15 March, the New Zealand Corps attacks from the north. It takes Castle Hill and Gurkhas reach Hangman's Hill below the abbey, but German paratroopers hold the ruins around the Continental Hotel and rain floods the craters, stopping the tanks. The battle is called off on 23 March. At Anzio a last German attack near Cisterna has failed in early March, and both sides dig in for two months of trench warfare under constant shellfire.

At 23:00 on 11 May some 1,600 guns open the fourth battle. The French Expeditionary Corps breaks through the Aurunci Mountains, British XIII Corps crosses the Rapido, and on 18 May the Polish II Corps raises its flag over the abbey ruins. The Canadians breach the Hitler Line on 23 May, the day VI Corps breaks out of the Anzio beachhead towards Cisterna. On 25 May patrols from the two fronts meet near Borgo Grappa, ending the isolation of the beachhead.

phases.t: 26 May – 4 June · the turn to Rome
phases.p: Instead of driving on to Valmontone to block the German Tenth Army's retreat along Route 6, Clark turns most of VI Corps north-west against the Caesar Line in front of Rome. The 36th Division slips through on Monte Artemisio on 30–31 May and the line collapses. Much of the Tenth Army escapes north through the mountains. US troops enter Rome on 4 June, two days before the Normandy landings push Italy off the front pages.

name: D-Day and Normandy: from the beaches to Falaise
intro: Five divisions landed from the sea and three from the air on 6 June. It then took the Allies seven weeks of attritional fighting in the hedgerows and around Caen to break out, and four more to trap the German armies in the Falaise pocket.

phases.p: Shortly after midnight the British 6th Airborne Division seizes the Orne bridges and the US 82nd and 101st Airborne drop, widely scattered, behind Utah. From 06:30 the US 4th Division lands at Utah with light losses, while at Omaha the 1st and 29th Divisions are pinned on the beach for hours before small groups climb the bluffs. Rangers scale Pointe du Hoc. The British and Canadians land on Gold, Juno and Sword; the 21st Panzer Division's counter-attack reaches the sea between Juno and Sword, but Caen is not taken.

The beachheads join up and the Americans take Carentan on 12 June. A British armoured thrust round the flank of Caen is stopped at Villers-Bocage on 13 June. VII Corps cuts the Cotentin peninsula on 18 June and turns north; the great storm of 19–22 June wrecks the Mulberry harbour off Omaha, and Cherbourg falls on 26–29 June with its port demolished. At the end of the month Operation Epsom pushes over the Odon west of Caen and draws in the SS panzer divisions.

After heavy bombers devastate much of the city, the British and Canadians take northern Caen on 9 July. Operation Goodwood, launched east of the Orne on 18 July with three armoured divisions, is stopped below Bourguébus ridge with heavy tank losses, but it keeps most German armour facing the British. The Americans grind through the bocage and take St-Lô on 18–19 July. On 25 July, after carpet bombing that also kills American troops, Operation Cobra breaks the German line west of St-Lô.

The US 4th Armored Division reaches Avranches on 30–31 July, and Patton's Third Army, activated on 1 August, pours through the gap into Brittany and east towards Le Mans. On 7 August Hitler's counter-attack at Mortain, Operation Lüttich, is stopped by the 30th Division on Hill 314 and by Allied fighter-bombers. The Canadians launch Operation Totalize towards Falaise on the night of 7–8 August, and US XV Corps swings north to Argentan, where Bradley halts it on 13 August.

The Canadians attack again in Operation Tractable on 14 August and take Falaise on 16–17 August. The Germans withdraw east through the narrowing gap between Trun and Chambois under constant artillery and air attack. On 19 August the Polish 1st Armoured Division and the US 90th Division meet at Chambois; Polish units on Hill 262 at Mont-Ormel hold off attacks from inside and outside the pocket until relieved on 21 August, when the gap is sealed. Some 50,000 Germans are captured.

name: Operation Market Garden
intro: Montgomery's plan was to lay a carpet of airborne troops along some 100 km of road and push XXX Corps up it to cross the Rhine at Arnhem. Every bridge had to be taken intact, and the whole corridor depended on a single road.

phases.p: In daylight on Sunday 17 September the largest airborne operation yet begins. The US 101st Airborne lands between Eindhoven and Veghel, but the Germans blow the Son bridge over the Wilhelmina Canal. The 82nd takes the Grave bridge and the Groesbeek heights, but not the Nijmegen road bridge. The British 1st Airborne lands some 10 km west of Arnhem, and only Frost's 2nd Battalion reaches the north end of the road bridge. At 14:35 XXX Corps attacks from the Meuse–Escaut canal and reaches Valkenswaard by nightfall.

The Guards Armoured Division reaches Eindhoven on 18 September; engineers bridge the canal at Son overnight and the tanks reach Nijmegen on the 19th. There the road bridge is held by SS troops in the Valkhof and Hunner Park. At Arnhem the rest of the 1st Airborne fails to break through to Frost along the river road near St Elisabeth's Hospital and falls back to a perimeter at Oosterbeek. Bad weather delays reinforcements, and German armour attacks the corridor at Son.

At about 15:00 on 20 September paratroopers of the 504th Parachute Infantry Regiment cross the 400 m-wide Waal in canvas assault boats west of the bridges, under heavy fire. As they seize the north ends, Grenadier Guards tanks rush the road bridge at dusk, but the advance halts for the night. At Arnhem, Frost's force, out of ammunition, is overrun by the morning of 21 September. That evening the Polish 1st Independent Parachute Brigade drops near Driel, south of the Rhine.

phases.t: 22–26 September · the corridor cut and Operation Berlin
phases.p: German attacks from both sides cut the corridor at Veghel on 22 September and again near Koevering on 24–25 September, holding up supplies and reinforcements. The 43rd Division reaches Driel, but attempts to ferry Poles and the 4th Dorsets across the Rhine fail. On the night of 25–26 September about 2,400 men are evacuated from the Oosterbeek perimeter across the river; more than 6,000 are captured. The Nijmegen bridgehead is held, but the Rhine is not crossed until March 1945.

name: The Battle of the Bulge
intro: Hitler's last great offensive in the west aimed to split the Allies by driving through the thinly held Ardennes to Antwerp. Low cloud grounded Allied aircraft, but stubborn American defence on the shoulders and at the road junctions of St Vith and Bastogne fatally slowed the attack.

phases.p: At 05:30 on 16 December three German armies attack along some 130 km of front. In the north the 6th SS Panzer Army is blocked by the 2nd and 99th Divisions at Krinkelt-Rocherath and on Elsenborn ridge, though Kampfgruppe Peiper breaks through the Losheim gap and murders some 84 American prisoners at Baugnez near Malmedy on 17 December. In the centre two regiments of the new 106th Division are surrounded on the Schnee Eifel and surrender on 19 December, and Manteuffel's panzers overrun the 28th Division on the Our.

The 7th Armored Division and remnants of other units hold St Vith until 21 December, then withdraw west of the Salm on 22–23 December. Bastogne, held by the 101st Airborne, Combat Command B of the 10th Armored Division and other units, is surrounded by 21 December; on the 22nd McAuliffe answers a German surrender demand with 'Nuts!'. Peiper, out of fuel, is trapped at La Gleize. Panzer spearheads bypass Bastogne and push west towards the Meuse.

With the skies clearing from 23 December, Allied aircraft drop supplies into Bastogne and strike the German columns. The 2nd Panzer Division reaches Foy-Notre-Dame, a few kilometres from the Meuse at Dinant, but it is out of fuel; on Christmas Day the US 2nd Armored Division destroys its spearhead around Celles, with British armour guarding the Meuse bridges. Peiper's men slip away from La Gleize on foot. At 16:50 on 26 December tanks of Patton's 4th Armored Division break through at Assenois and relieve Bastogne.

Hitler throws more divisions at the Bastogne corridor, and on 1 January launches Operation Nordwind in Alsace and a mass air attack on Allied airfields. The First Army attacks from the north on 3 January and the Third Army from the south; in deep snow they meet at Houffalize on 16 January. St Vith is retaken on 23 January, and by 28 January the line is back roughly where it started. The Americans have lost some 19,000 killed; the Germans have spent their last reserves in the west.

name: Berlin: from the Seelow Heights to the Reichstag
intro: Two Soviet fronts raced each other to Berlin while a third attacked further north. The battle began with a frontal assault on the Seelow Heights and ended sixteen days later with the red flag over the Reichstag and the surrender of the city.

phases.t: 16–19 April · the Oder and the Seelow Heights
phases.p: At 03:00 Moscow time on 16 April Zhukov's 1st Belorussian Front opens a huge bombardment from the Küstrin bridgehead and switches on searchlights that mostly dazzle its own troops. The German 9th Army has pulled back to the Seelow Heights, and the attack bogs down in the flat Oderbruch below. Zhukov throws in his tank armies too early; only on 19 April is the last defence line broken. To the south Konev's 1st Ukrainian Front crosses the Neisse and advances much faster.

Stalin lets Konev turn his tank armies north towards Berlin. Rybalko's 3rd Guards Tank Army reaches the army high command headquarters at Zossen on 21 April, and Soviet guns begin shelling the city. The 9th Army is cut off in the forests south-east of Berlin. On 25 April troops from the north and south meet at Ketzin, closing the ring round the city, and the same day Konev's 58th Guards Rifle Division meets the US 69th Infantry Division on the Elbe at Torgau.

Inside the ring Weidling's LVI Panzer Corps, Volkssturm and Hitler Youth defend the city district by district. Chuikov's 8th Guards Army crosses the Landwehr Canal towards the government quarter, while the 3rd Shock Army fights over the Moltke bridge towards the Reichstag. Wenck's 12th Army attacks from the west and gets as far as Ferch near Potsdam, and the trapped 9th Army breaks out westwards through Halbe at terrible cost. Hitler kills himself on 30 April; that night Soviet soldiers raise a flag on the Reichstag.

Fighting goes on inside the Reichstag into 2 May. Goebbels' attempt to negotiate a ceasefire is rejected, and early on 2 May General Weidling surrenders the Berlin garrison to Chuikov. Survivors of the 9th Army reach Wenck's lines near Beelitz, and both armies fall back to the Elbe to surrender to the Americans. Some 134,000 defenders go into captivity. Germany capitulates unconditionally at Reims on 7 May and again in Berlin-Karlshorst on 8 May.
